questions.q: What is the capstone project built across Lessons 29-31?
options: A five-tool multi-agent orchestration system
A support agent with two tools — a read-only get_order and a consequential issue_refund — that applies the safety patterns from Chapters 4 and 5
A chatbot with no tool access at all
A tool that only generates marketing copy
questions.explain: The capstone is deliberately scoped to one read-only tool and one consequential tool, small enough to finish while giving every Chapter 4-5 control real work to do.

questions.q: According to this lesson, why is the capstone scoped to just two tools instead of five or more?
options: The Claude API only allows a maximum of two tools per agent
More tools would make the project look more impressive, so two is purely a time-saving shortcut with no other reasoning

The point is to prove every control (checkpoint, logging, budget, sandboxing) is actually wired up and working, not just described — a two-tool agent with everything working teaches more than a five-tool agent with none of it working
Two tools is a hard technical limitation of the course platform
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly argues that depth (every control real and functioning) beats breadth (more tools but none of the safety work actually implemented).

questions.q: Which lesson's design does the capstone's approval checkpoint on issue_refund directly apply?
options: Lesson 12's ReAct pattern
Lesson 19's approval checkpoint design (what a reviewer needs to see, and approve/reject mapped onto tool_result and is_error)
Lesson 6's tool schema description guidance only, with no checkpoint
Lesson 3's basic tool-use fundamentals, with no changes
questions.explain: The capstone's checkpoint on issue_refund is a direct, concrete application of the approval checkpoint design built in Lesson 19, including handling rejections as a tool_result with is_error.

questions.q: Why does the capstone's get_order tool not need an approval checkpoint, using the rule of thumb from Lesson 18?
options: Because get_order is read-only and not irreversible, costly, or inherently low-confidence — the three signals Lesson 18 uses to decide whether a tool call needs human approval
Because all tools in a capstone project are automatically exempt from approval
Because get_order costs more in tokens than issue_refund
Because read-only tools are not supported by the tool_use mechanism
questions.explain: Lesson 18's rule of thumb flags irreversible, costly, or low-confidence actions for approval; a read-only lookup like get_order has no such consequence, so gating it would only add friction with no safety benefit.

questions.q: According to this lesson's chapter-to-build-step mapping, which earlier chapter's content becomes the capstone's stopping conditions, cost budget, sandboxing, and audit log?
options: Chapter 1's agent loop fundamentals
Chapter 3's agent architectures and patterns
Chapter 5's agent safety and guardrails content
Chapter 2's tool calling and function design content
questions.explain: The lesson's mapping places stopping conditions, budgets, sandboxing, and audit logging — all from Chapter 5 — directly onto the corresponding parts of the capstone build.
